analysis.one_liner: Requires a seven-day waiting period before most firearm purchases.
analysis.headline: The bill would have required a 7-day wait before someone could take home a gun, with penalties up to 5 years in prison, but it died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a crime — punishable by a fine, up to 5 years in prison, or both — to hand over a gun to an unlicensed buyer until at least 7 calendar days after the buyer first asked to take possession. The point is to put a pause between a decision to buy a gun and actually getting one. Some transfers are exempt, such as temporary use at a shooting range, hunting, or a loan while the owner is present. It never got past its first referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk from impulsive gun violence — buyers going through a crisis, domestic disputes, or moments of anger — who the waiting period is designed to give time to reconsider or be stopped. Law enforcement also gains a clearer rule on when a transfer is legal. Family and community members exposed to impulsive shootings benefit from the pause.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of impulsive gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Creates a mandatory 7-calendar-day pause between when an unlicensed buyer offers to take a firearm and when the seller may legally hand it over, inserted as a new section of the federal gun-control law (18 U.S.C. 922).
Backs the waiting period with criminal penalties — a fine of up to $250,000, up to 5 years in prison, or both — for knowingly transferring a gun before the wait is up.

Includes practical exceptions so the wait does not block legitimate uses: temporary transfers at a shooting range, for hunting, trapping, farm pest control, or fishing, or while the owner stays present, provided the seller has no reason to believe the buyer will misuse the gun or is legally barred from having one.
The rule takes effect 90 days after enactment, giving sellers and buyers time to adjust before penalties begin.

analysis.who_pays: Gun buyers who want a firearm immediately, including people buying for self-defense on short notice, would have to wait a week before taking possession. Gun dealers and private sellers would bear the compliance burden and potentially lose sales made on impulse, and any seller who ignores the wait faces fines up to $250,000 and up to 5 years in prison.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun buyers and sellers wanting immediate transfers

drawbacks.text: The 7-day wait applies to essentially every retail and private sale to an unlicensed buyer, including people who feel they need a gun urgently for protection — a common objection to waiting periods is that they delay law-abiding buyers facing an imminent threat, such as someone who has just been threatened or stalked.

The penalties are severe relative to the act: a seller who hands over a gun one day early faces the same fine of up to $250,000 and up to 5 years in prison as for more serious knowing violations, leaving little room for honest mistakes.

Opponents of waiting periods generally argue that people determined to harm themselves or others can find other means during the pause, and that a federal one-size-fits-all wait overrides state laws that already set their own rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a deliberate cooling-off window aimed at impulsive shootings and self-harm, with exemptions that spare range use, hunting, and supervised loans. The cost falls on buyers who want a gun right away for protection and on dealers who must hold sales for a week and could lose business. The strongest objection — that a person in immediate danger cannot wait seven days for a defensive firearm — is real and the bill offers no expedited option for that situation. Whether the pause saves lives was never tested legislatively because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan introduced the bill on March 29, 2023, joined by Reps. Ann Kuster and David Trone, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
That referral was the last action ever recorded: the full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Only two other members signed on as cosponsors over the bill's nearly two-year life, and the House never considered it again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Anyone who opposed a federal waiting period — including gun sellers and buyers who prefer to take a firearm home the same day — kept the status quo, because the bill never received even a committee hearing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of federal waiting periods; gun sellers

for.name: Rep. Elissa Slotkin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House on March 29, 2023.

for.name: Reps. Ann Kuster and David Trone
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's two cosponsors when it was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 29, 2023 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat with no further action for the rest of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's three supporters were all Democrats, and the committee controlled by Republicans never acted on it.

industries.note: A 7-day mandatory hold on transfers to unlicensed buyers would delay and likely cut into same-day sales, including impulse purchases, and expose dealers to fines up to $250,000 or 5 years in prison for selling early. The industry's interest in immediate sales runs against the bill's goal of slowing access to guns.

Waiting periods can reduce overall purchase volume, so gun makers stood to lose some sales. The bill contains no buyback, licensing, or manufacturing restrictions, so the impact on manufacturers is smaller than on dealers.
